## SCORE Values

### **Learning**
We believe that bioinformatics is a constantly evolving field, and that ongoing learning and professional development is essential to staying up-to-date. We encourage members to share their knowledge and experiences with each other, and to seek out opportunities for continued learning.

### **Accessibility**
We believe that access to bioinformatics support should be available to everyone. We strive to create a welcoming and inclusive environment where all members can feel comfortable asking for help and contributing to the group.

### **Collaboration**
We believe that working together is key to achieving success in bioinformatics. We value the diversity of perspectives and backgrounds that each member brings, and we encourage open communication and the sharing of ideas.

### **Integrity**
We believe in conducting ourselves with honesty and professionalism in all our interactions. We hold ourselves to high ethical standards and respect the privacy and confidentiality of all members.

### **Empathy**
We believe in approaching each other with empathy and kindness. We understand that bioinformatics can be a challenging and sometimes frustrating field, and we strive to support each other through these difficulties.

## Create Institutions Dataframe, Define the Order of Graph + Legend, and Set the Color Palette
### **Note:** Set the **same factor** on two different dataframes
### **Note:** I asked **ChatGPT** to help me select the color palette

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "gantt_code2.png")`)

## ggplot2 code
### **Note:** geom_segment() **AND** geom_line()
### **Note:** labs(color = "") sets the legend title
### **Note:** scale_y_discrete() sets the order of mentors

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "gantt_code3.png")`)

## **Code** to produce the **Gantt chart**
### Yes, **I asked chatGPT** to clean up and annotate the code!

```{r eval=FALSE, error=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=TRUE}

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# Load data
df <- read.csv(here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "data", "JWNMentors.csv"))

# Define institution list
institutions <- c(
  "University of Washington",
  "Oregon Health & Science University",
  "University of Southern California"
)

# Categorize mentors
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    MentorType = ifelse(Mentor %in% institutions, "Institution", "Individual")
  )

# Reshape data
g.gantt <- df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = 3:4, names_to = "state", values_to = "date") %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(date, "%m/%d/%Y"))

# Create summarized timeline for institutions
g.gantt_combined <- g.gantt %>%
  filter(MentorType == "Institution") %>%
  group_by(Stage) %>%
  summarise(
    start_date = min(date[state == "Start"]),
    end_date = max(date[state == "End"]),
    Mentor = "Institution"
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Define factor levels for Stage
stage_levels <- c(
  "University of Washington",
  "Oregon Health & Science University",
  "University of Southern California",
  "Undergraduate",
  "Graduate School",
  "Postdoc",
  "Junior Faculty"
)

g.gantt$Stage <- factor(g.gantt$Stage, levels = stage_levels)
g.gantt_combined$Stage <- factor(g.gantt_combined$Stage, levels = stage_levels)

# Define y-axis order
desired_order <- rev(c(
  "Institution", "Staffan Bench", "Benjamin Hall", "Nabil Alkayed",
  "Paul Barnes", "Sanjiv Kaul", "David Ellison",
  "Susan Gurley", "Janos Peti-Peterdi"
))

# Define color mapping
desired_colors <- c(
  "University of Washington" = "#32006e",
  "Oregon Health & Science University" = "#575e60",
  "University of Southern California" = "#990000",
  "Undergraduate" = "#C5692E",
  "Graduate School" = "#FEB359",
  "Postdoc" = "#435F90",
  "Junior Faculty" = "#B47E83"
)

# Create plot
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = g.gantt_combined,
    aes(x = start_date, xend = end_date, y = Mentor, yend = Mentor, color = Stage),
    size = 10
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = g.gantt,
    aes(x = date, y = Mentor, color = Stage),
    size = 10
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL, title = "Mentors", color = "Institution and Career Stage") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = desired_order) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = desired_colors, na.value = "gray")

```

# Main Theme: **Reporting Data**

## Best Practices for Reporting Data for Manuscripts
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_001.png")`)

### Pipeline
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_002.png")`)

### 1. Raw Sequencing Files (FASTQ)
-These are the raw output files directly generated by the sequencing machine (e.g., Illumina NovaSeq, NextSeq, etc.): <br>
-In single-cell/single-nuclei RNA sequencing, you obtain short reads from mRNA that was already reverse transcribed into cDNA. <br>

Main files
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_003.png")`)


Why are these files comprressed (.gz)? <b>
<br>
FASTQ files are huge. They’re compressed with gzip to reduce size. A single experiment can easily generate hundreds of GBs. <br>
<br>
What happens next?<br>
<br>
These files are passed to preprocessing pipelines, like: Cell Ranger, STARsolo (bulk RNA-seq), Kallisto | Bustools (pseudoalignment), etc.


### 2. Preprocessing Files (via Cell Ranger, etc.)
After generating the raw FASTQ files, the next step is to process the data using a pipeline like:<br>
Cell Ranger (10X Genomics)
These tools: <br>
-Match reads to individual cells using barcodes
-Deduplicate reads using UMIs <br>
-Align the reads to a genome or transcriptome <br>
-Build the count matrix: genes × cells <br>
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_003.png")`)

Output folder structure (Cell Ranger) <br>
Cell Ranger generates several files and folders after processing single-cell RNA-seq data. The key outputs are: <br>
https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/cell-ranger/latest/analysis/outputs/cr-outputs-gex-overview
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_004.png")`)

Outputs compatible with Seurat, Scanpy, IGV, and downstream tools can be used with CellBender, Alevin, or custom workflows <br>


A) Filtered Feature Matrix (typically under outs/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/):
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_005.png")`)


Output file format: Which one should you use? MEX vs HDF5 (.h5)? <br>
Both formats contain the same information: <br>
A gene × cell expression matrix, with barcodes and features. <br>
The difference is in the file structure and format: <br>
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_006.png")`)



B) raw_feature_bc_matrix/ <br>
-Same structure as filtered_feature_bc_matrix, but: <br>
-Includes all barcodes, even:Empty droplets, Damaged cells, Low-quality barcodes <br>
<br>
Why is it useful? <br>
Re-analyze using your own custom filtering, Identify ambient RNA contamination

C) QC and Summary Reports: 
-web_summary.html: Interactive summary with plots (genes per cell, mitochondrial %, etc.)
                  An interactive report viewable in any browser. Shows:
                  Total number of estimated cells
                  Reads per cell
                  Median genes per cell
                  % mitochondrial gene expression
                  Sequencing saturation
                  Clustering preview (if applicable)
                  Useful for checking: If the run worked, How deep was the sequencing, General quality of data (need it for publishing)
- metrics_summary.csv: Tabular summary of sequencing and mapping statistics

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_007.png")`)
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_008.png")`)


D) BAM (Binary Alignment/Map) Files:  possorted_genome_bam.bam and .bam.bai
BAM files store sequencing reads aligned to a reference genome in binary format.
-possorted_genome_bam.bam: contains genome/transcriptome-aligned reads + unassigned ones.
                          Includes aligned and unaligned reads if Feature Barcode libraries are present (e.g., Antibody, CRISPR,                                 Multiplexing).

The cellranger multipipeline produces:
unassigned_alignments.bam: reads not assigned to any sample.
sample_alignments.bam: reads assigned to specific samples.

Use cases:Troubleshooting unassigned reads, Converting BAM back to FASTQ, Each read includes Chromium barcodes (cellular & molecular).
You can load this into: IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer), Custom scripts to explore gene-level alignments


E) cloupe.cloupe:
This is a binary file made specifically for: Loupe Cell Browser (by 10X Genomics)--> It’s provided by 10x Genomics as a free tool to explore data generated with their technologies, especially .cloupe files from Cell Ranger.
It lets you:Visually explore clusters, See gene expression per cluster, Annotate cell types manually, Perform interactive marker gene analysis, Not required for programmatic analysis, but great for biologists or presentations.
https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/loupe-browser/latest
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_009.png")`)


### 3. Downstream Analysis (Seurat, etc)

Processed Data Formats:
  - .rds (Seurat): Includes count matrix, metadata, UMAP, clusters
  - .h5ad (Scanpy): Same as above but in Python format
  - metadata.csv: Per-cell information (cluster, % mito, etc.)
  - degs.csv: Differentially expressed genes between clusters or conditions
  - umap.png, violin_plot.png: Visual outputs from analysis
  
### 4. Optional Files (?) and Documentation for Code Sharing: Best Practices for Sharing Projects (Guidelines?)
These files help others understand, run, and reproduce your project (on GitHub or similar platforms).

Projects should include additional files to support:
  Data Sharing:Make your datasets accessible (e.g., via GEO or public repositories).
  Reproducibility:Include scripts and environment files to allow others to rerun your analysis exactly.
  Collaboration:Clear documentation helps others understand and contribute to your project.

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_010.png")`)

## Data: GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) – Public data sharing platform for genomics

What is GEO?
GEO is a public repository managed by the NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information).
It's used to store and share high-throughput gene expression data, including:
  Microarray
  Bulk RNA-seq
  Single-cell/snRNA-seq
  Multi-modal (CITE-seq, spatial transcriptomics)
  
If you're publishing your data, journals will typically require that you upload your sequencing data to a public archive like GEO or ArrayExpress.
GEO helps you:
  Fulfill publishing requirements
  Promote reproducibility and transparency
  Share your data with the scientific community
  Let others reuse your data 
  
What’s included in a typical GEO submission?
When you submit a dataset to GEO, you're usually uploading:

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_011.png")`)

Where to find GEO in papers ?

![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_012.png")`)


GEO Structure: The 3 layers
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_013.png")`)
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_014.png")`)
Example Use Case:
Let’s say you want to download an existing single-cell dataset to practice your pipeline:
Search on GEO for keywords like "mouse kidney single-cell"
Open a GSE entry (e.g. GSE165385)
Download: matrix.mtx.gz, barcodes.tsv.gz, genes.tsv.gz. Or download .h5ad or .rds directly if available
Then you can load it into Seurat or Scanpy and start exploring.

In your paper or project:
“Data available at GEO under accession number GSE228367.”


A .tar file is an archive format that bundles multiple files and folders into a single file, without compressing them.
Think of it like a ZIP file, but without compression by default.
Very common in Linux/Unix systems and in bioinformatics for packaging datasets.
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_015.png")`)
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_016.png")`)
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_017.png")`)

Cell bender: https://github.com/broadinstitute/CellBender
CellBender is a Python-based tool developed by the Broad Institute to clean single-cell RNA-seq data.
  Removes ambient RNA (background noise) from droplet-based scRNA-seq data (e.g., from 10x Genomics).
  Uses deep learning to distinguish real cells from noise.
  Improves data quality before clustering or analysis in tools like Scanpy or Seurat.
  Especially helpful for samples with high ambient contamination (e.g., frozen tissues or nuclei).
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_018.png")`)

## Code: Github
GitHub – Code, documentation, and collaboration platform
![](`r here::here("Week 3 Reporting Findings", "Images", "IMG_020.png")`)

What is GitHub?
GitHub is a version-controlled code hosting platform.
It’s perfect for managing your analysis scripts, notebooks, and documentation.
It’s built on Git, which allows you to track every change you make to a file.
Use GitHub Releases to tag versions (e.g., "v1.0 – preprint version")
Add a LICENSE (Reference) file to clarify how others can use your code
Add badges (optional) to show R/Python versions, citation info, etc.

## Shiny App

What is a Shiny App?
A Shiny App is an interactive web application built using the R programming language. It allows you to turn your R scripts, data visualizations, and statistical models into a web interface, without needing to write HTML, JavaScript, or CSS.
 Why is it useful in single-cell/snRNA-seq analysis?
In single-cell or single-nuclei RNA-seq projects, a Shiny App allows scientists, clinicians, or collaborators (even without coding skills) to:
-Explore clusters and cell types 
  -Visualize expression of marker genes
  -Interact with UMAP or t-SNE plots
  -Compare experimental conditions.
  -Download plots or data tables easily
It turns static results into a dynamic data exploration tool.
How does it work?
You perform your analysis in R (e.g., with Seurat).
You use the shiny package to build the user interface and server logic.
The app runs as a web page, which users can explore without touching code.

https://ellisonlab.shinyapps.io/dct_shinycell/
https://ellisonlab.shinyapps.io/tal_shinycell/
